label: Against Heresies: Book I — Translator and historical edition notes (part 4)

blocks.text: [^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-301]: We here follow the text as preserved by Hippolytus. The Latin has, “a certain man in Asia.”
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-302]: [This is disputed by other primitive authorities.]
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-303]: Rev. ii. 6 .
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-304]: [Comp. cap. xxv. 3.]
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-305]: We here follow the amended version proposed by the Benedictine editor.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-306]: A promise never fulfilled: comp. book iii. 12, and Euseb., Hist. Eccl. , v. 8.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-307]: [ Rev. xii. 9 .]
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-308]: [The whole casuistical system of the Trent divines, De Matrimonio , proceeds on this principle: marriage is licensed evil.]

[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-309]: Harvey supposes this name to be derived from two Syriac words, meaning “God in a Tetrad.” Matter again derives it from two Hebrew words, denoting “Daughter of the Lord.”
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-310]: Both the text and meaning are here altogether doubtful.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-311]: Harvey refers to the cabbalistic books in explanation of this and the following names, but their meanings are very uncertain.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-312]: Various explanations of this word have been proposed, but its signification remains altogether doubtful.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-313]: Ex. xx. 5 ; Isa. xlv. 5, 6 .
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-314]: The punctuation is here difficult and doubtful.

[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-315]: The probable meaning of this and the following names is thus given by Harvey: Ialdabaoth, Lord God of the Fathers ; Iao, Jehovah ; Oreus, Light ; Astanphæus, Crown ; Sabaoth, of course, means Hosts ; Adoneus, Lord ; and Eloeus, God . All the names are derived from the cabbalistic theology of the Jews.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-316]: Hence their name of Ophites, from ὄφις , a serpent .
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-317]: The Latin has evertisse , implying that thus Nous was more degraded.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-318]: Gen. i. 26 .
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-319]: That is, from Ialdabaoth, etc. [ Philastr. ( ut supra ), Oehler, i. p. 38.]
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-320]: There is constant reference in this section to rabbinical conceits and follies.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-321]: A name probably derived from the Hebrew נערה , girl , but of the person referred to we know nothing.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-322]: We here follow the emendation of Grabe: the defection of Prunicus is intended.

[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-323]: The Latin here is “ex quibus,” and the meaning is exceedingly obscure. Harvey thinks it is the representative ἐξ ὦν ( χρόνων ) in the Greek, but we prefer to refer it to “Judæos,” as above. The next sentence seems unintelligible: but, according to Harvey, “each deified day of the week had his ministering prophets.”
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-324]: The common text inserts “et incorruptibili Æone,” but this seems better rejected as a glossarial interpolation.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-325]: 1 Cor. xv. 50 . The Latin text reads “apprehendunt,” which can scarcely be the translation of κληρονομῆσαι in the Greek text of the New Testament.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-326]: That is, Christ and Jesus.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-327]: The text of this sentence is hopelessly corrupt, but the meaning is as given above.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-328]: According to Harvey, Hystera corresponds to the “passions” of Achamoth. [Note the “Americanism,” advocate used as a verb.]
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-329]: The text is here imperfect, and the translation only conjectural.
[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-330]: [ Cant. ii. 15 ; St. Luke xiii. 32 .]

[^irenaeus-against-heresies-ix-ii-331]: [Let the reader bear in mind that the Greek of this original and very precious author exists only in fragments. We are reading the translation of a translation; the Latin very rude, and the subject itself full of difficulties. It may yet be discovered that some of the faults of the work are not chargeable to Irenæus.]
